title: Smithland: Zachariah Cox's town on the Cumberland
summary: Smithland began in the late 1790s as land speculator Zachariah Cox's trading post where the Cumberland meets the Ohio. Gen. James Wilkinson had Cox arrested, but the town, named for Cox's scout John Smith, was platted in 1805.
bodyMarkdown:
Smithland sits where the Cumberland River pours into the Ohio, one of the best trading spots in the western country. Its founder never got to enjoy it. [Zachariah Cox](/people/#zachariah-cox) picked the site, sent a friend to hold it, and then watched a U.S. general wreck his plans.

## A speculator from Georgia

Cox was a surveyor and land speculator who, by [the Encyclopedia of Alabama's account](https://encyclopediaofalabama.org/article/zachariah-cox/), was born about 1765. Between 1789 and 1795 he organized Georgia land companies that bought millions of acres along the Tennessee River in the Yazoo land sales. When Georgia's new legislature voided those sales in 1796, his company collapsed, and he looked for a new venture farther west.

## John Smith holds the point

In his own later account, Cox wrote that [in 1796 he had the country at the mouth of the Cumberland explored and improved](https://archive.org/stream/documentsrelatin00coxirich/documentsrelatin00coxirich_djvu.txt) by Capt. [John Smith](/people/#john-smith-smithland). In April 1797, at Knoxville, he announced a commercial settlement there. Passing through Frankfort in January 1798, he told Gov. [James Garrard](/people/#james-garrard) what he intended and promised to obey the laws. [The settlement took Smith's name](https://grokipedia.com/page/Smithland,_Kentucky).

## Wilkinson's opposition

Downriver at Fort Massac sat Gen. [James Wilkinson](/stories/gen-james-wilkinson-kentuckys-agent-13/), who had plans of his own for a trading settlement in cooperation with the Spanish. He persuaded the president and the secretary of war that Cox was [building a boat for piracy and for war against the Indians](https://web.archive.org/web/20261101122631/http://livingstoncountyky.org/history.php). Cox slipped past Fort Massac anyway and went down the Mississippi.

On August 18, 1798, he was arrested at Natchez. He escaped to New Orleans, was jailed again in Nashville, and was cleared at trial, but he lost his company. Back at the Cumberland, he found his goods had been taken. He petitioned Congress in 1803; it agreed that his arrest had been illegal but paid him nothing. He disappears from local records about then, and he died in Virginia around 1838.

## A plat and a river town

The settlers he left behind stayed. Smithland was [laid out on a plat in 1805](https://grokipedia.com/page/Smithland,_Kentucky), though the plat was not recorded until 1837: six blocks along the river and two blocks back. Lots in town are still located by it. Boats stopped there to transfer passengers and produce between the two rivers, and the town got a rough name as a brawling river landing.

When the [New Madrid earthquakes](/stories/the-new-madrid-earthquakes-in-kentucky-1811-12/) struck in December 1811, residents ran into the streets as chimneys fell.

By the 1830s Smithland had sawmills, a boatyard that built steamboats, a dock company, a brickyard, an iron works and a newspaper, the Smithland Herald. When Crittenden County was split off in 1842, the Livingston County seat moved to Smithland, and a new courthouse went up in 1845.

## Kentucky today

Smithland is still the Livingston County seat, a town of about 240 people on the original grid. The 1845 courthouse is on the National Register, and the Gower House, an early inn on the riverfront, still stands. The map pin marks the state marker on the courthouse lawn.
